## Prediction using Neural Networks

As a second predictive approach we forecast taxi demand — pickups per spatial unit and time bucket — with feed-forward neural networks (NNs). Demand is not an additive function of its drivers: location, hour, calendar effects and local context (points of interest, weather) interact strongly and non-linearly, the effect of an hour depending on the neighbourhood and the effect of a holiday on the hour. A linear model such as our ridge benchmark captures only some of this and shifts the burden onto manual feature engineering, whereas a network discovers the relevant combinations directly during training. We judge the networks against two benchmarks: a ridge regression and, more importantly, a historical-mean predictor (mean `trip_count` per cell × hour-of-day in the training period). The latter is a demanding baseline, and whether the added flexibility of a network actually beats this cheap lookup — and at which resolutions — is what this chapter sets out to establish.

### Evaluation method

Our client wants to understand ride-hailing demand dynamics in Chicago, so we frame the evaluation around the operational questions a fleet operator would ask: can simple NNs predict demand reliably, and is the gain over the near-free historical mean large enough to justify building, tuning and retraining them? Which data serves demand prediction best — hexagons or community areas, hourly or coarser buckets? We answer these along two dimensions: first by comparing the three architectures within a fixed resolution, where MAE and R² together give a precise, intuitive read on performance; and second by comparing across temporal (1 h, 2 h, 6 h, 24 h) and spatial resolutions (community areas vs. H3 hexagons), where we lean on MAPE and R² for scale-independence while keeping MAE as a tangible reference for non-technical readers.

Behind these headline figures we record RMSE, NRMSE (raw and log scale) and a zero-demand accuracy score for empty cells, and we retain per-epoch learning curves to diagnose overfitting. To gauge whether a network's error distribution differs from a benchmark's beyond chance, we run a Wilcoxon signed-rank test against each. It is worth stating plainly what this test can and cannot do: it indicates whether two error distributions differ on this particular sample, not whether the operator should deploy a network. That decision is a cost–benefit one, taken up in the conclusion; the significance test only orients us toward configurations worth costing out.

### Architecture and training

We compare three fully connected architectures that differ only in capacity — a **baseline** (2 hidden layers × 64 units), a **deeper** model (8 × 64) and a **wider** model (2 × 256) — each evaluated across the four time buckets and two spatial units. After sweeping optimizers, activations and losses, we settled on the configuration that gave the best performance for the least added complexity: ReLU activations with He/Kaiming-normal initialization (which balances weight variances across layers and reduces the chance of unstable starts), and stochastic gradient descent with momentum. A cell's spatial identity — a community area or H3 hexagon — enters not as a one-hot vector but as a jointly learned 16-dimensional embedding concatenated with the standardized numeric features, so that similar locations sit near one another in a learned latent space; a reserved "unknown" bucket lets the model degrade gracefully on locations unseen at inference. The scaler and embedding vocabulary are fitted on the training split only, and target-leaking columns are dropped.

The most consequential choice is the training objective, because demand is over-dispersed, zero-inflated count data. MSE would assume symmetric constant-variance errors and allow negative predictions; a Poisson likelihood respects the counts but assumes variance equals mean, which ours violates. For the 1 h, 2 h and 6 h models we therefore minimise the **negative binomial (NB2) negative log-likelihood**, which models the excess variance explicitly. The network emits a log-rate that is exponentiated back to the count scale, and this link is also its weakness: because `exp()` grows steeply, a small log-space error becomes a large count error, and at daily aggregation — where demand averages ~180 (CA) to ~420 (hex) per day — a minor overshoot can explode into millions of predicted trips and destabilise training. The 24 h models are consequently trained on **MAE over the log1p scale** instead; their loss values and learning curves are therefore not directly comparable to the finer horizons, and only the raw-count evaluation metrics below can be compared across all buckets.

Learning rate and weight decay are tuned per architecture by a two-stage grid search — a coarse sweep over `2e-5`–`8e-2` to locate the right decade, then a fine sweep within it — each candidate evaluated with a short patience of 5 and a single seed to keep the search affordable, before the winner is retrained under the full schedule. Overfitting is held in check by that decoupled weight decay and by early stopping on validation loss (patience 10, best-weight restoration). The data are split 70/15/15; the split is positional (`shuffle=False`), so validation and test are the tail of the dataframe rather than a random draw despite the `SPLIT="random"` label in the code.

### Expectations

We formulated five hypotheses before training. (1) The NNs should clearly beat the linear ridge, since demand responds non-linearly to hour, location and weather. (2) They should at least match the historical mean by learning the cell × hour interaction, and surpass it by using information the lookup cannot — weekday, holidays, weather deviations. (3) More capacity should help modestly, with the deep variant most exposed to optimization instability. (4) The NN advantage should be largest at fine temporal granularity, where samples are plentiful and day-to-day fluctuation matters, and shrink or vanish at daily buckets, where data volume collapses and the stable mean pattern dominates. (5) Hyperparameters — the learning rate above all — should matter more than architecture.

### Model Comparison

The table reports test-set R² and MAE for the historical-mean benchmark and the best tuned NN per configuration (NB2 loss unless noted).

| Spatial unit | Bucket | Benchmark R² (MAE) | Best NN R² (MAE) | Best model |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Hex (H3 res 6) | 1 h | 0.833 (7.24) | **0.849 (6.40)** | deeper, tuned |
| Hex (H3 res 6) | 2 h | 0.840 (13.88) | **0.880 (11.83)** | deeper, tuned |
| Hex (H3 res 6) | 6 h | **0.858** (38.81) | 0.845 (36.41) | wider, tuned |
| Hex (H3 res 6) | 24 h | **0.876** (132.3) | 0.10 (203.1) | deeper, tuned |
| Community areas | 1 h | — | 0.851 (3.07) | baseline, tuned |
| Community areas | 2 h | — | 0.834 (6.02) | deeper, tuned |
| Community areas | 6 h | — | 0.788 (18.93) | deeper, tuned |
| Community areas | 24 h | — | 0.727 (76.60) | deeper, tuned |

Four findings stand out. **Tuning dominates architecture** (hypothesis 5): untuned, every architecture lands far below its tuned counterpart, and the deep model occasionally produces strongly negative R² from a handful of exploded predictions — while its deviance-based D² stays around 0.85, showing these are tail artefacts of the exponential link, not globally broken models. **The granularity pattern matches hypothesis 4**: the NNs beat the historical mean clearly at 1–2 h, roughly tie at 6 h (better MAE, worse R²), and fail at 24 h, where only ≈8k training rows remain — too few for a network, while the lookup keeps improving as the averaging horizon grows. **Capacity helps only after tuning**: the tuned deeper model is strongest at fine granularity but the most fragile untuned. Finally, two ablations tracked the earlier feature analysis — removing the weather block at 2 h did not hurt (weather had near-zero permutation importance), and sigmoid matched ReLU at 1 h.

### Exemplary walkthrough (H3 resolution 6, hourly)

The hourly hexagon configuration illustrates the pipeline. It covers 33 hexagons over 289k cell-hours; 35.8 % of test rows are zero-demand and mean test demand is 17.6 trips. Ridge reaches R² = 0.59 — beaten by every tuned network (hypothesis 1) — while the historical mean sets the real bar at R² = 0.833, MAE = 7.24. An untuned baseline (lr $5\cdot10^{-5}$) reaches only R² ≈ 0.78, undertrained; grid search moves it to lr 0.04, weight decay $5\cdot10^{-3}$ and R² = 0.834, level with the benchmark. The tuned deeper model (lr $6\cdot10^{-3}$, weight decay $3\cdot10^{-3}$) reaches **R² = 0.849, MAE = 6.40** — ≈12 % lower mean error than the benchmark, achieved precisely where the lookup is blind: day-to-day deviations from the average hex-hour pattern.

### Conclusion and interpretation for the business case

Neural networks add real predictive value exactly at the granularity operations need. For repositioning idle taxis, planning shifts and anticipating local surges, hourly-to-two-hourly hexagon forecasts are the actionable resolution, and there the tuned networks lower mean error by 12–15 % (≈6.4 vs. 7.24 trips per hex-hour against a mean of 17.6) — precise enough to rank cells for repositioning, with the NB model's strictly positive outputs directly readable as expected pickups. So yes, the networks can predict demand reliably and beat the cheap benchmark — but only where it matters (hypotheses 1 and 2).

Whether that gain is *worth implementing* is a cost question the significance tests cannot answer, so it is worth weighing the two sides explicitly. On the benefit side the edge is real but bounded: a few R² points and ~12–15 % MAE, confined to fine hex-level horizons, and zero or negative beyond 6 h. On the cost side a network is markedly more expensive than the mean across its whole life: a per-configuration two-stage learning-rate and weight-decay search to build it; an exponential link fragile enough that an untuned model can be worse than the free benchmark, demanding careful re-tuning whenever the data shift; recurring retraining, divergence monitoring and serving infrastructure to operate it; and a loss of the full transparency the lookup offers. The historical mean, by contrast, costs essentially nothing to compute, needs no tuning and stays interpretable. The gain therefore only justifies the network where fine-grained accuracy carries enough operational value to outweigh these recurring costs — i.e. hourly/2-hourly hex-level repositioning. At 6 h and daily horizons (hypothesis 4) the mean is as good or better on accuracy *and* dominant on cost, and should simply be used; on the data question, this makes fine spatial units paired with fine time buckets the only resolution where modelling effort pays off.

Several caveats and open items bound this reading. Most runs use a single seed, so small R² gaps should not be over-read; the daily models optimise a different loss on a different scale, so their training curves are not comparable; and the NB2 likelihood addresses over-dispersion in the mean only, not exact zero-demand probabilities. We also did not benchmark training or inference **speed** or **scalability**, which leaves real-time retraining viability unsettled, and we did not convert accuracy into money — the decisive input for the cost–benefit above. Closing that gap is the natural next step: express error in missed rides and idle vehicles per unit of MAE, test whether a network's complexity beats a simpler learner such as an SVM per unit of operational cost, map where the model fails most (new areas, rare events, unusual weather) and how risky those failures are, and identify what data the operator must collect once live to keep the models accurate. For deployment we recommend a pragmatic hybrid: the historical hex-hour mean as an always-available, near-free fallback — or, in future work, an input feature — with the tuned NB network supplying the fine-grained hourly corrections wherever the repositioning value justifies its upkeep.
